issue.title: Should AI stand in for one of the two experts who read a breast screen?
issue.question: Should the NHS let an AI take the place of one of the two human experts who read a woman's breast screen, and who should decide?
issue.summary: Recruitment has started at Cambridge, the first of 30 hospitals in EDITH, a trial of AI in NHS breast screening, according to BBC reporting carried by the Copenhagen Post. Today two human experts read each screen. Women in the trial are randomly put into one of three groups: two experts as now, or AI used in one of two ways, either to review after the expert or to rate the risk before the experts read. The trial's information says "All images will be looked at by at least one human expert", and a woman can decline AI and have two experts read her images without it. Government support is £11 million, and the trial is expected to run about three years.
issue.slot_reason: The NHS had not come up yet in the simulation, and the start of the EDITH breast screening trial was in the UK news that day. Of that day's stories, it asked the clearest values question: who decides whether a machine can stand in for a human check.

bench.title: Keep two experts for some women; test AI with one expert
bench.answer: The Health Secretary would sign a rule for the 30 EDITH hospitals. No trust may cut reading jobs or hours because of the trial; time saved goes to shorter waits. Volunteers are placed by lot: two experts as now, or AI with one expert. Letters say which. Scan data stays in the NHS; no private firm may profit from it. Provisional fail: the AI group finds one in ten fewer cancers, or more cancers showing up between screens, than the two-expert group. First check at 12 months, including waits. Stops 31 December 2029 unless Parliament renews it. Leaves out women under 50 or over 71, and any who decline AI. Two-expert women get no less than today.

bench.title: NHS-owned scan software, women told their group, staff can stop it
bench.answer: Inside EDITH's volunteer sites, the Health Secretary would sign a rule: the NHS owns the software and every scan, and no firm may keep or sell them. Volunteers are picked by lot: two experts as now, or one expert plus the NHS-owned AI. Each woman is told her group. A woman can say no and keep two experts. No post is cut; time saved goes to shorter waits. Staff and women sit on a panel that can switch it off. Fail: if AI finds more than 1 in 100 fewer cancers than two experts, checked at 12 months, it stops. Ends 31 December 2029 unless Parliament renews it. Leaves out women who decline and women outside the 30 sites.

bench.title: Give local women the brake on AI screening
bench.answer: Your scan, your choice. Trial replacing one reader only with willing women, assigned by lot against two human readers. Each NHS unit needs approval from a local patient panel drawn by lot; its clinical director signs. Explain each woman's allocation. Keep staff, a named human contact and two readers for anyone declining. Contracts must forbid commercial reuse of scans. Publish results by ethnicity, age and deprivation, counting women missing from the trial. Provisional failure: fewer cancers found, more cancers between screens, or median waits not cut 10%. Review waits after six months; stop on 30 November 2029 unless Parliament renews after independent safety review. Patient panels can stop participation earlier. No national rollout on inconclusive evidence.

issue.title: When a big chain fails, who looks after its workers and towns?
issue.question: When a big high street chain is failing, what should the government do for its workers and the towns it leaves behind?
issue.summary: Poundland, a chain of about 600 stores and 12,000 staff, is in sale talks. City AM reported on 20 November 2026 that a preferred bid was due to be chosen by 25 November, and that a pause on creditors' demands was due to end on 26 November. If a whole-company bid fails, the stores, staff and stock could be auctioned to rivals. City AM said its owner, Gordon Brothers, made about £20m available in the week of 9 November, and that ITV News had reported £60m of sales cash still out of reach.

bench.title: Workers paid first and fast, whoever buys or auctions the stores
bench.answer: The government has said it is keeping its options open (s2). This answer would make any sale or store auction (s1) conditional on workers being paid first, with no public money for owners. The Insolvency Service already aims to pay eligible employee claims within 6 weeks (s3); the government would make that a hard limit. Contractors, who now queue as creditors (s4), would get the same route through a rule change. Success: every eligible claim, contractors included, is paid within 6 weeks, and the department publishes the count of claims paid and days taken.

bench.title: Give staff and towns first call on stores before any auction
bench.answer: If a whole-company bid fails, Poundland's stores, staff and stock could be auctioned to rivals [s1]. Instead, the government, which has said it is keeping its options open [s2], would give staff groups and local councils a short first right to take over any store due to close, with the Insolvency Service paying owed wages and notice directly [s3]. No public money would go to the owner or bosses; that limit had 51 backers among simulated citizens. Contractors, who must otherwise queue as creditors [s4], would be paid in the same round. It worked if workers were paid within 6 weeks [s3], and most closing stores were reopened or reused rather than left empty.

bench.title: Let workers and towns buy a fresh start
bench.answer: If Poundland is sold in pieces, which could happen [s1], government should fund a local rescue scheme. Workers and local shoppers would jointly own rescued shops, with one vote each. Councils would offer capped loans only where a plan shows sales can cover wages, rent and repayments. Money would buy shop assets, never shares in the failing owner. The same scheme would advance unpaid wages within two weeks and fund training where shops cannot survive. Each town would publish costs, repayments and jobs kept after a year. Success means workers paid promptly and shops covering their bills without repeat support.

issue.title: The EU deal: food, carbon and young people, and who pays for student fees
issue.question: How much should Britain give up to get closer trade and travel with the EU, and who should pay if EU students get home fees?
issue.summary: At the UK-EU summit in Brussels on 20 November 2026 the two sides agreed a food and farm trade deal, a link between their carbon markets and a youth scheme for 18 to 31 year olds. The government says the package could add up to 0.5% to UK GDP by 2040, about £17 billion a year. The youth scheme is capped and visa-based, with no access to benefits. Both sides also agreed to work towards a deal on tuition fees within six months; EU officials want EU students to pay UK home rates, and the UK disputes that this is linked to the rest of the deal.

bench.title: Home fees for EU students, but capped, reciprocal and costed in public
bench.answer: Keep the current fee system and universities; change the terms of the tuition deal due within six months (s4). Home-rate fees would apply to EU students only inside a fixed yearly cap on places, set by ministers and kept separate from places for UK students, so none are cut. The deal would start only when the EU gives UK students equal fees. The Treasury would publish the yearly gap and fund it from a named budget line, not from NHS or school money. Parliament would review it after three years, and the cap shrinks or the deal ends if the gap passes the published limit. It worked if UK places hold, the gap stays inside the limit, and UK students use the reciprocal rate. The Russell Group warns that any cut to EU student fees would put pressure on UK places (s4).

bench.title: A joint fees board, not a trade-off behind closed doors
bench.answer: Take the fee question out of the wider trade talks and give it to a joint UK-EU fees board with equal seats for UK students, EU students and universities, plus a fixed budget. The two governments would set that up within weeks, inside the six months they have already agreed for a fees deal (s4). Times Higher Education reports EU officials saying the rest of the deal hangs on fees, and the UK side disputing that (s4), so a separate board lets the food, carbon and youth parts go ahead. The Russell Group warns that any fee cut would put pressure on UK places (s4), and 26 simulated citizens set a limit of no free places paid by taxpayers, so the board's pot must be named and capped. It worked if the rest of the deal is not held up, the fee rate is published, and UK places do not fall.

bench.title: Trade access, but let students steer the fee bargain
bench.answer: In this simulation, Britain should accept shared food and carbon rules for easier trade, but offer home fees only with equal terms for UK students abroad. Fee talks are still open (s4). Parliament should set that bargain. Elected student and staff boards at each university should check its costs. Employers wanting to recruit through the youth scheme should fund any fee gap through a charge for taking part. No signed funding, no fee concession. Publish the accounts each year. Judge success by cheaper food, shorter border waits, students travelling both ways, falling emissions and no lost university places or courses.

gate.verdict: Two of three pass the limits plainly (A on money, C on subjects and standards); none shows it would cut absence, because no source tests that. Facts cannot settle who should decide what Years 7 to 9 are for.

jury.question: Who should decide what Years 7 to 9 are for: the government, the inspectors, or each school's own families and teachers?
options: Government keeps the rule, with inspection and a funded grant
Each school's families and teachers decide, in the open
Elected school councils with a family majority, plus a national floor
Leave schools alone and let parents choose between them
jury.ruling: Each school's families and teachers decide, in the open. Five of the twelve jurors wanted the choice made by the people in the building, with plans and results published.

reasons.text: I studied late and wish someone had asked what the early years were for. Let the school say, in the open.
Keep the rule. In my day the exam board set it and it held. Add the money so nobody loses subjects.
Councils and panels are more committees. Parents should pick a school and leave when it lets them down.
Families should have the majority, but a national floor stops some schools doing nothing at all.

minister.trial: In 10 secondary schools that now start GCSE courses before Year 10, a panel of teachers, parents and Year 7 to 9 pupils, drawn by lot, signs off a published three-year plan for Years 7 to 9. The department funds the panel's time. Plans, timetables and absence rates are public.
minister.fail_number: Persistent absence in Years 7 to 9 in the 10 schools rising above their own 2026 rate (target: lower), or any school dropping a subject or cutting staff to fund the plan (target: none).
minister.statement: Quick quiz. Who knows best what Years 7 to 9 are for: the exam board, the department, or the people in the building? The jury leaned to the building. Five of twelve, not a landslide. So I'm signing one small thing. Ten schools, a panel drawn by lot, a plan on the school's own door. The department pays for the time, so nobody robs music to do it. The trade-off: some panels may pick the exam treadmill anyway. If they do, they have to say why, out loud.
